def nearest_expiry_table(q, dte_targets, max_expiries):
    base = q.groupby("expiry").agg(dte=("dte_days", "median"), n=("quote_id", "size")).reset_index()
    base = base[base["n"] >= 7].copy()
    chosen = []
    used = set()
    for target in dte_targets:
        z = base[~base["expiry"].isin(used)].copy()
        if z.empty:
            break
        z["dist"] = (z["dte"] - float(target)).abs()
        row = z.sort_values(["dist", "n"], ascending=[True, False]).iloc[0]
        chosen.append(row["expiry"])
        used.add(row["expiry"])
        if len(chosen) >= max_expiries:
            break
    return chosen


def bucket_ok(g, need_left=2, need_atm=2, need_right=2):
    left = int((g["k"] <= -0.12).sum())
    atm = int((g["k"].abs() <= 0.05).sum())
    right = int((g["k"] >= 0.08).sum())
    return left >= need_left and atm >= need_atm and right >= need_right


def choose_k_grid_quotes(q, dte_targets, k_targets, *, max_expiries=6, min_strikes=7, require_buckets=False, need_left=2, need_atm=2, need_right=2, min_vega_use=None, max_rel_spread_use=None, label="panel"):
    pieces = []
    vega_floor = min_vega if min_vega_use is None else float(min_vega_use)
    spread_cap = max_rel_spread if max_rel_spread_use is None else float(max_rel_spread_use)
    for expiry in nearest_expiry_table(q, dte_targets, max_expiries):
        g0 = q[q["expiry"].eq(expiry)].copy().sort_values("k")
        chosen = []
        used = set()
        for kt in k_targets:
            g = g0[~g0["quote_id"].isin(used)].copy()
            if g.empty:
                continue
            j = (g["k"] - float(kt)).abs().idxmin()
            chosen.append(g.loc[j])
            used.add(g.loc[j, "quote_id"])
        if not chosen:
            continue
        s = pd.DataFrame(chosen).drop_duplicates("quote_id")
        s = s[(s["relative_spread"] <= spread_cap) & (np.abs(s["vega"]) >= vega_floor) & (s["mid"] > 0)].copy()
        if require_buckets and not bucket_ok(s, need_left, need_atm, need_right):
            extras = []
            for mask, need in [
                (g0["k"] <= -0.12, need_left),
                (g0["k"].abs() <= 0.05, need_atm),
                (g0["k"] >= 0.08, need_right),
            ]:
                pool = g0[mask & ~g0["quote_id"].isin(s["quote_id"])].copy()
                pool = pool[(pool["relative_spread"] <= spread_cap) & (np.abs(pool["vega"]) >= vega_floor) & (pool["mid"] > 0)]
                pool = pool.sort_values(["relative_spread", "k"])
                extras.append(pool.head(max(0, need)))
            add = pd.concat(extras, ignore_index=False) if extras else g0.head(0)
            s = pd.concat([s, add], ignore_index=False).drop_duplicates("quote_id")
        if len(s) >= min_strikes and ((not require_buckets) or bucket_ok(s, need_left, need_atm, need_right)):
            pieces.append(s.sort_values("k"))
    out = pd.concat(pieces, ignore_index=True) if pieces else q.head(0).copy()
    out = out.sort_values(["expiry", "k"]).reset_index(drop=True)
    out.attrs["label"] = label
    return out


def panel_bucket_table(q, label):
    rows = []
    for expiry, g in q.groupby("expiry", sort=True):
        rows.append({
            "panel": label,
            "expiry": expiry,
            "dte_days": float(g["dte_days"].median()),
            "quotes": int(len(g)),
            "left_wing": int((g["k"] <= -0.12).sum()),
            "near_atm": int((g["k"].abs() <= 0.05).sum()),
            "right_wing": int((g["k"] >= 0.08).sum()),
            "tail_count": int((g["k"].abs() >= 0.14).sum()),
            "k_min": float(g["k"].min()),
            "k_max": float(g["k"].max()),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

title: 11. Stochastic Volatility Models and Model-Risk-Aware Option Relative Value
text:
11) Merton Jump-Diffusion
The Merton jump-diffusion model extends a lognormal diffusion by adding random jumps. In forward form, a simplified risk-neutral log process can be written as:
\[
d\log F_t=\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2-\lambda\kappa_J\right)dt+\sigma dW_t+J_t dN_t
\]
where:

\(\sigma\) is the continuous diffusion volatility,
\(N_t\) is a Poisson jump counter,
\(\lambda\) is the expected number of jumps per year,
\(J_t\) is the log jump size when a jump occurs,
\(J_t\sim N(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2)\),
\(\kappa_J=E[e^{J_t}-1]\) is the average percentage jump effect.

The compensator \(-\lambda\kappa_J\) is essential. Without it, adding jumps would change the risk-neutral drift of the forward. Under risk-neutral pricing, the discounted forward must be a martingale, so the drift has to offset the average jump effect.
If jumps are usually negative, then \(\mu_J<0\). If jump sizes are uncertain, then \(\sigma_J\) is positive. Both raise the value of OTM puts because the left tail becomes fatter.
For example, if \(\lambda=0.4\), the model expects about 0.4 jumps per year, or one jump every 2.5 years on average. If \(\mu_J=-0.15\), the typical jump is strongly negative in log terms. Even if such jumps are rare, short-dated OTM puts can become much more valuable because they pay exactly in those rare states.

Merton as a Poisson Mixture of Black Prices
Merton’s jump-diffusion model has a useful pricing interpretation. Conditional on the number of jumps \(n\) over the option life, log returns are still normally distributed, but with shifted mean and extra variance from jumps. The probability of \(n\) jumps is Poisson:
\[
P(N_T=n)=e^{-\lambda T}\frac{(\lambda T)^n}{n!}
\]
So the option price can be interpreted as a weighted sum of Black-like prices over possible jump counts:
\[
V^{Merton}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} P(N_T=n)\,V^{Black}(\text{adjusted parameters for } n)
\]
The exact adjustment depends on convention, but the intuition is simple. The no-jump scenario gets the largest probability when \(\lambda T\) is small. One-jump and two-jump scenarios get smaller probabilities, but they can contribute a lot to OTM option values because their payoffs are convex.
This is why rare jumps matter so much for options. A 5% probability of a large downside move can have a large effect on a deep OTM put, even if it barely changes the average forward.


Merton and Short-Maturity Smile Convexity
Jump models are especially important at short maturities. Diffusion moves scale with \(\sqrt{T}\), while jump arrival probability scales with \(T\).
For a diffusion:
\[
\text{typical move} \sim \sigma\sqrt{T}
\]
For a Poisson jump:
\[
P(\text{one jump})\approx \lambda T
\]
At very short maturities, a continuous diffusion needs very high volatility to create deep tail probability. A jump model can put a small amount of probability mass far away from the center. That can make deep OTM options valuable without raising the whole ATM volatility too much.
This is exactly why Merton is used as a tail diagnostic. If the market’s short-dated left wing is much richer than ATM Black can explain, a negative jump component can bridge that gap. It won’t fit every detail, but it tells us whether discontinuity is an important part of the surface.


Jump Parameters and Tail Shape
The three jump parameters affect the tail differently.
The intensity \(\lambda\) controls how often jumps arrive. Higher \(\lambda\) raises the probability of one or more jump events:
\[
P(N_T\ge1)=1-e^{-\lambda T}
\]
The mean jump \(\mu_J\) controls the direction and average size. A negative \(\mu_J\) creates downside skew. A positive \(\mu_J\) would make upside calls more expensive.
The jump volatility \(\sigma_J\) controls the dispersion of jump sizes. Larger \(\sigma_J\) makes both tails fatter because jumps can be more extreme in either direction.
For SPX, the fitted \(\mu_J\) is negative, which matches crash-protection demand. For BTC, Merton later becomes even more competitive, but the reason is different: BTC can have strong two-sided jump behavior and less stable liquidity, so a jump distribution can explain a lot of the option surface.


Merton Calibration Objective
Merton is calibrated in price space. For selected quotes \(i=1,\ldots,n\), we minimize weighted pricing residuals:
\[
\min_\theta \sum_{i=1}^n \omega_i\left(\frac{V^{Merton}_i(\theta)-V^{mkt}_i}{\epsilon_{V,i}}\right)^2
\]
with:
\[
\theta=(\sigma,\lambda,\mu_J,\sigma_J)
\]
Each residual is divided by the quote’s price uncertainty \(\epsilon_{V,i}\). This matters because a $2 pricing error on a wide-tail option is less serious than a $2 error on a tight, liquid quote.
In this implementation, Merton acts as a jump-tail diagnostic bridge. It is much simpler than Heston and Bates, and it calibrates fast. If it improves tail pricing compared with ATM Black, that tells us jumps are useful for explaining the observed short-maturity wings.


Jump Compensation in Plain Terms
The compensator \(\lambda\kappa_J\) can feel abstract, so here is the financial logic.
If jumps have average multiplicative effect \(E[e^J]\), then:
\[
\kappa_J=E[e^J-1]=e^{\mu_J+\frac{1}{2}\sigma_J^2}-1
\]
If jumps are negative on average, \(\kappa_J<0\). If we simply added those jumps without adjusting the drift, the forward would drift downward under the risk-neutral measure. That would violate the martingale condition for a forward.
So the drift includes:
\[
-\lambda\kappa_J
\]
If \(\kappa_J\) is negative, this term is positive. The continuous part drifts slightly upward to offset the average negative jumps. The total risk-neutral process remains correctly centered, while the distribution becomes more negatively skewed and fat-tailed.
This is a good example of how option models separate mean from shape. The risk-neutral forward expectation stays anchored, but the distribution becomes more crash-sensitive.


Show code
seed = 1107
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
n_demo = 120_000
sigma_demo = 0.20
lam_demo = 1.2
mu_j_demo = -0.055
sig_j_demo = 0.12
tau_j_demo = 30.0 / ann_days
r_no_jump = (-0.5 * sigma_demo ** 2 * tau_j_demo) + sigma_demo * np.sqrt(tau_j_demo) * rng.normal(size=n_demo)
n_jump = rng.poisson(lam_demo * tau_j_demo, size=n_demo)
r_jump = r_no_jump + n_jump * mu_j_demo + np.sqrt(n_jump) * sig_j_demo * rng.normal(size=n_demo)
z_path = rng.normal(size=90)

Show code
@njit
def n_cdf(x):
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0)))


@njit
def black_px_nb(is_call, df, f_mean, strike, var):
    if var <= 1e-12:
        payoff = max(f_mean - strike, 0.0) if is_call else max(strike - f_mean, 0.0)
        return df * payoff
    sig = math.sqrt(var)
    d1 = (math.log(max(f_mean, 1e-300) / max(strike, 1e-300)) + 0.5 * var) / sig
    d2 = d1 - sig
    if is_call:
        return df * (f_mean * n_cdf(d1) - strike * n_cdf(d2))
    return df * (strike * n_cdf(-d2) - f_mean * n_cdf(-d1))


@njit
def merton_one(is_call, fwd, strike, tau, df, sigma, lam, mu_j, sig_j, max_jumps):
    jump_var = sig_j * sig_j
    kappa_j = math.exp(mu_j + 0.5 * jump_var) - 1.0
    mean_n = max(lam * tau, 0.0)
    wt = math.exp(-mean_n)
    px = 0.0
    for n in range(max_jumps + 1):
        var = sigma * sigma * tau + n * jump_var
        f_n = fwd * math.exp(-lam * kappa_j * tau + n * mu_j + 0.5 * n * jump_var)
        px += wt * black_px_nb(is_call, df, f_n, strike, var)
        if n < max_jumps:
            wt *= mean_n / (n + 1.0)
    return px


@njit(parallel=True)
def merton_px(is_call, fwd, strike, tau, df, sigma, lam, mu_j, sig_j, max_jumps):
    n = strike.size
    out = np.empty(n, dtype=np.float64)
    for i in prange(n):
        out[i] = merton_one(is_call[i], fwd[i], strike[i], tau[i], df[i], sigma, lam, mu_j, sig_j, max_jumps)
    return out

def fit_merton(q):
    is_call = q["option_type"].eq("call").to_numpy(dtype=np.bool_)
    f = q["forward"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k_strike = q["strike"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

    root_wt = np.sqrt(q["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    near_iv = pd.to_numeric(q.loc[q["k"].abs() <= 0.05, "iv_mid"], errors="coerce").replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).dropna()
    all_iv = pd.to_numeric(q["iv_mid"], errors="coerce").replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan).dropna()
    atm_sigma = float(near_iv.median()) if len(near_iv) else float(all_iv.median()) if len(all_iv) else 0.20
    lo = np.array([0.03, 0.00, -0.50, 0.01])
    hi = np.array([1.20, 6.00, 0.25, 0.85])

    def err(p):
        px = merton_px(is_call, f, k_strike, tau, df, p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3], 45)
        r = root_wt * (px - y) / eps
        return np.where(np.isfinite(r), r, 1e3)

    starts = [np.array([atm_sigma, 0.40, -0.04, 0.10]), np.array([0.85 * atm_sigma, 1.25, -0.08, 0.16]), np.array([1.10 * atm_sigma, 0.15, -0.02, 0.06]), np.array([0.70 * atm_sigma, 2.50, -0.12, 0.22])]
    best = None
    for p0 in starts:
        t0 = tic()
        res = optimize.least_squares(
            err,
            np.minimum(np.maximum(np.nan_to_num(p0, nan=0.5 * (lo + hi), posinf=hi - 1e-5, neginf=lo + 1e-5), lo + 1e-6), hi - 1e-6),
            bounds=(lo, hi),
            loss="soft_l1",
            f_scale=1.0,
            max_nfev=160,
            xtol=1e-7,
            ftol=1e-7,
        )
        item = {"res": res, "cost": float(res.cost), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
        if best is None or item["cost"] < best["cost"]:
            best = item
    return best["res"].x, best["res"].success, best["seconds"], best["res"].nfev, lo, hi

The calibrated Merton parameters are:

\(\sigma\approx 0.099\),
\(\lambda\approx 0.386\),
\(\mu_J\approx -0.146\),
\(\sigma_J\approx 0.126\).

The interpretation is economically clear: continuous volatility is low compared with the surface wings, while the model adds rare negative jumps to explain downside protection. A jump intensity around 0.39 means less than one jump per year on average, but the average log jump is materially negative. That is a natural SPX shape: ordinary daily variation is moderate, but the market prices crash states.
Fit quality is reasonable for this compact price-space panel: weighted price RMSE around 3.33, weighted IV RMSE around 0.0092, median absolute IV error around 0.0044, and P90 around 0.0323. The tail diagnostic is valid and tail error is about 0.0133. The Merton curve improves the tail fit compared with a simple expiry-ATM Black benchmark, where the tail weighted price RMSE is about 16.58 versus 3.25 for Merton.


Merton Parameter Interpretation in Annual Units
The fitted jump intensity \(\lambda\approx 0.386\) is annualized. For a 30-day option, the approximate probability of one or more jumps is:
\[
1-e^{-0.386(30/365)}\approx 3.1\%
\]
For a 90-day option:
\[
1-e^{-0.386(90/365)}\approx 9.1\%
\]
These probabilities are small but not negligible. For OTM puts, a few percent probability of a large negative jump can dominate value.
The fitted \(\mu_J\approx -0.146\) corresponds to a typical multiplicative jump around:
\[
e^{-0.146}-1\approx -13.6\%
\]
The jump volatility \(\sigma_J\approx 0.126\) means jump sizes are dispersed around that mean. So the model is not simply saying that one fixed crash size is priced. It is saying the risk-neutral jump-size distribution is centered materially negative with a wide range of possible outcomes.

The Merton plot shows the model capturing the broad left-wing richness much better than a flat ATM-vol model. That’s the whole reason jump diffusion is included. It provides a compact way to explain why OTM puts have higher implied volatility.
The residual panels show that Merton is still limited. A single jump distribution across the selected panel can’t fully match every maturity and wing point. It can thicken tails, but it doesn’t create a full stochastic term structure of variance. That limitation is the bridge into Heston: instead of adding only discontinuous moves, we allow variance itself to be random and mean reverting.


Why Merton Can Fit Tails Without Fitting the Whole Surface
Merton has only four main parameters here, so it can’t match every maturity-specific smile feature. Its strength is narrower: it can add fat tails.
The model changes the terminal distribution from a single lognormal into a mixture. The left tail gets heavier when jumps are negative or volatile. OTM puts then rise in price.
But Merton lacks stochastic variance. That means it doesn’t naturally create a realistic variance term structure. If the market has different short- and medium-term skew dynamics, Merton has to approximate them through one jump intensity and one jump-size distribution.
That is why Merton’s tail improvement is meaningful but limited. It tells us jump risk is a useful ingredient. It doesn’t mean a pure jump-diffusion is enough for the whole surface.

text:
12) Heston: Stochastic Variance as a State Variable
Heston is the central stochastic-volatility model in this project. The risk-neutral dynamics are:
\[
\frac{dF_t}{F_t}=\sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t^F
\]
\[
dv_t=\kappa(\theta-v_t)dt+\xi\sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t^v
\]
with:
\[
dW_t^F dW_t^v=\rho dt
\]
The parameters are:








Parameter
Meaning
Financial role




\(v_0\)
initial variance
level of current instantaneous variance


\(\kappa\)
mean-reversion speed
how quickly variance moves back toward long-run variance


\(\theta\)
long-run variance
variance level the process reverts toward


\(\xi\)
vol-of-vol
how violently variance itself moves


\(\rho\)
spot-vol correlation
creates leverage-effect skew



This is a much richer model than Black-Scholes. Volatility isn’t a constant parameter. It is a random process. A low \(v_t\) today doesn’t guarantee low volatility tomorrow because the variance process can receive shocks. The square-root term \(\sqrt{v_t}\) makes variance shocks state-dependent: when variance is high, variance itself is more volatile.
The mean-reversion term \(\kappa(\theta-v_t)\) pulls variance toward \(\theta\):

if \(v_t<\theta\), the drift is positive,
if \(v_t>\theta\), the drift is negative.

This produces volatility clustering without letting variance wander forever.

Heston’s Instantaneous Variance Distribution
The variance process:
\[
dv_t=\kappa(\theta-v_t)dt+\xi\sqrt{v_t}dW_t^v
\]
is a square-root diffusion. The \(\sqrt{v_t}\) term does two things:

it keeps volatility-of-variance smaller when variance is low,
it allows large variance fluctuations when variance is already high.

The conditional mean over a horizon \(u\) has a simple form:
\[
E[v_{t+u}\mid v_t]=\theta+(v_t-\theta)e^{-\kappa u}
\]
This equation is extremely useful. If \(v_t\) is above \(\theta\), the expected future variance decays toward \(\theta\). If \(v_t\) is below \(\theta\), it rises toward \(\theta\). The speed is controlled by \(\kappa\).
For example, if \(\kappa=2\), the half-life of a variance shock is approximately:
\[
\frac{\log 2}{\kappa}\approx 0.35 \text{ years}
\]
So variance shocks are expected to decay over a few months, not instantly. That is why Heston can create term-structure effects: short options see current variance strongly, while longer options average over future mean reversion.


Heston Term Structure Through Expected Variance
The conditional mean equation can be integrated to approximate expected average variance over the option life:
\[
E\left[\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T v_sds \mid v_0\right]
=
\theta+\frac{v_0-\theta}{\kappa T}(1-e^{-\kappa T})
\]
This expression explains how Heston creates an implied-volatility term structure. Short maturities are heavily influenced by \(v_0\). Long maturities move closer to \(\theta\) because the variance process has more time to mean revert.
If \(v_0<\theta\), longer options can have higher average variance than very short options. If \(v_0>\theta\), the opposite can happen. In the fitted Heston output, \(v_0\) is much lower than \(\theta\), so the model uses a rising expected variance component, while skew and curvature come from \(\rho\) and \(\xi\).
This is a powerful idea: the term structure is not imposed maturity by maturity. It emerges from the variance state and mean-reversion process.


Heston and the Leverage Effect in Covariance Form
The spot-vol correlation can also be read through covariance. From the Heston equations:
\[
d\log F_t \approx \sqrt{v_t}dW_t^F
\]
and:
\[
dv_t \approx \xi\sqrt{v_t}dW_t^v
\]
The instantaneous covariance is:
\[
\text{Cov}(d\log F_t,dv_t)=\xi v_t \rho\,dt
\]
If \(\rho<0\), this covariance is negative. That means negative returns tend to come with positive variance shocks. The strength of the effect increases with \(\xi\) and with current variance \(v_t\).
This is why \(\rho\) and \(\xi\) work together. A mildly negative \(\rho\) with small \(\xi\) produces weak skew. A strongly negative \(\rho\) with high \(\xi\) produces strong skew. The fitted Heston model has both fairly negative \(\rho\) and high \(\xi\), so it is using the leverage channel aggressively.


How Heston Creates Skew
The correlation \(\rho\) is the skew engine. If \(\rho<0\), negative forward shocks tend to occur with positive variance shocks. In equity index markets, that matches the leverage effect: when equities fall, volatility often rises.
In small-step terms:
\[
d\log F_t \approx -\frac{1}{2}v_tdt+\sqrt{v_t}dW_t^F
\]
and:
\[
dv_t \approx \kappa(\theta-v_t)dt+\xi\sqrt{v_t}dW_t^v
\]
If \(\rho=-0.7\) and the forward shock \(dW_t^F\) is negative, then \(dW_t^v\) tends to be positive. That means the price path falls while future variance rises. A put option benefits from both effects: the underlying moves toward the strike and volatility increases. This is why negative \(\rho\) produces downside skew.
The demo paths show both pieces. Variance paths mean-revert but can jump around because variance has its own Brownian shock. The correlated forward/variance path shows the forward and instantaneous volatility moving together in a way that a constant-volatility model can’t reproduce.


Integrated Variance and Option Prices
An option payoff depends on the terminal forward, but under stochastic volatility the terminal distribution is driven by the whole path of variance. The key path quantity is integrated variance:
\[
I_T=\int_0^T v_s ds
\]
Conditional on a variance path, the log-forward has variance roughly \(I_T\). So options care about the distribution of \(I_T\), not only the starting variance \(v_0\).
This is why Heston can create smiles. If integrated variance is random, the final return distribution becomes a mixture of normal distributions with different variances. Variance mixtures have fatter tails than a single normal distribution. Negative correlation \(\rho\) then makes the left tail even heavier because bad forward moves tend to occur with higher future variance.
A simple mental picture:

Black-76 uses one variance bucket.
Heston randomizes the variance bucket.
Negative \(\rho\) links the bucket size to the direction of the move.

That combination produces skew and smile while keeping the path continuous.


The Feller Condition
The Heston variance process is a square-root process. A classic condition for strict positivity is:
\[
2\kappa\theta \ge \xi^2
\]
We can summarize this with the Feller ratio:
\[
\text{Feller ratio}=\frac{2\kappa\theta}{\xi^2}
\]
If this ratio is above 1, the continuous-time process stays strictly positive under the classical condition. If it is below 1, variance can approach zero in theory, and numerical schemes need care.
This condition isn’t a simple “good/bad” label in calibration. Real market calibrations often violate it because the market wants high vol-of-vol \(\xi\) to fit steep smiles. A low Feller ratio says: the parameter set is using very aggressive variance randomness relative to mean reversion and long-run variance. We can still use it diagnostically, but we have to read it as a warning.


Monte Carlo Pricing Under Heston
Although Heston has a semi-closed-form characteristic-function solution, here we price it by Monte Carlo. For every path:

start at the current forward \(F_0\) and variance \(v_0\),
simulate correlated shocks \(dW^F\) and \(dW^v\),
update log-forward and variance through time,
compute the terminal payoff,
average discounted payoffs across paths.

The simulated forward update is approximately:
\[
\log F_{t+\Delta t}=\log F_t-\frac{1}{2}v_t\Delta t+\sqrt{v_t\Delta t}\,Z_F
\]
The variance update is:
\[
v_{t+\Delta t}=v_t+\kappa(\theta-\max(v_t,0))\Delta t+\xi\sqrt{\max(v_t,0)\Delta t}\,Z_v
\]
The use of \(\max(v_t,0)\) is a practical full-truncation-style protection. It prevents the square root from breaking when the Euler step makes variance slightly negative.
The Monte Carlo estimator is:
\[
\hat{V}=D\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} \text{payoff}^{(m)}
\]
and its standard error is:
\[
SE(\hat{V})=D\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\text{payoff})}{M}}
\]
This standard error is central to reading the residuals. If the model price is $0.40 away from the market but Monte Carlo standard error is $0.45, the residual is barely meaningful.


Common Random Numbers and Calibration Noise
Monte Carlo calibration can become unstable if every parameter trial uses new random numbers. The objective function would be noisy: a parameter vector might look better simply because it got luckier simulated paths.
To reduce this, we use common random numbers. The same random shock arrays are reused across parameter evaluations. Then the difference between two parameter vectors is mostly due to the parameters, not due to fresh simulation noise.
If the objective is:
\[
L(\theta)=\sum_i r_i(\theta)^2
\]
and \(r_i(\theta)\) is estimated by Monte Carlo, common random numbers make the estimated loss surface smoother. That helps least-squares optimization converge.
We also use antithetic shocks. If \(Z\) is a normal shock, we also simulate \(-Z\). Averaging the pair reduces simulation variance because positive and negative random fluctuations partially cancel. This doesn’t remove Monte Carlo error, but it makes the same number of paths more efficient.


Optimization Noise and False Parameter Precision
Monte Carlo calibrated parameters can look more precise than they really are. The optimizer returns a parameter vector, but that vector depends on:

selected quotes,
parameter bounds,
random path set,
number of paths,
time discretization,
objective scaling,
starting values.

If the MC standard error is large relative to pricing residuals, then small differences in objective value are not meaningful. Two parameter sets can produce prices that differ by less than simulation noise.
This is why Heston and Bates are labeled diagnostic. The parameter values are useful for economic interpretation, but we shouldn’t treat the last decimal as meaningful. A fitted \(\rho=-0.6286\) means “strong negative spot-vol correlation,” not “the true correlation is exactly -0.6286.”
The project reports MC standard errors because without them we could mistake simulation noise for model precision.

n_v_demo = 14

mc_paths_opt, mc_paths_final, mc_steps_per_year = 1024, 8192, 52
def shocks(n_path, n_step, salt):
    n_half = max(int(n_path) // 2, 2)
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed + salt)
    z1 = r.normal(size=(n_half, n_step))
    z2 = r.normal(size=(n_half, n_step))
    return np.vstack([z1, -z1]).astype(np.float64), np.vstack([z2, -z2]).astype(np.float64)

Show code
@njit(parallel=True)
def heston_px_mc(is_call, fwd, strike, tau, df, v0, kappa, theta, xi, rho, steps_per_year, z_s, z_v):
    n_quote = strike.size
    n_path = z_s.shape[0]
    px = np.empty(n_quote, dtype=np.float64)
    se = np.empty(n_quote, dtype=np.float64)
    rho2 = math.sqrt(max(1.0 - rho * rho, 1e-12))
    for i in prange(n_quote):
        n_step = max(1, int(math.ceil(tau[i] * steps_per_year)))
        dt = tau[i] / n_step
        sqrt_dt = math.sqrt(dt)
        s1 = 0.0
        s2 = 0.0
        for p in range(n_path):
            log_f = math.log(max(fwd[i], 1e-300))
            v = max(v0, 1e-12)
            for j in range(n_step):
                vp = max(v, 0.0)
                dw_s = z_s[p, j]
                dw_v = rho * z_s[p, j] + rho2 * z_v[p, j]
                log_f += -0.5 * vp * dt + math.sqrt(vp) * sqrt_dt * dw_s
                v = v + kappa * (theta - vp) * dt + xi * math.sqrt(vp) * sqrt_dt * dw_v
            ft = math.exp(log_f)
            payoff = max(ft - strike[i], 0.0) if is_call[i] else max(strike[i] - ft, 0.0)
            s1 += payoff
            s2 += payoff * payoff
        mean = s1 / n_path
        var = max(s2 / n_path - mean * mean, 0.0)
        px[i] = df[i] * mean
        se[i] = df[i] * math.sqrt(var / n_path)
    return px, se

def fit_heston(q):
    is_call = q["option_type"].eq("call").to_numpy(dtype=np.bool_)
    f = q["forward"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    k_strike = q["strike"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    tau = q["tau"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    df = q["discount_factor"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = q["mid"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    eps = np.maximum(q["calib_scale_px"].to_numpy(dtype=float), 0.02)
    root_wt = np.sqrt(q["weight"].to_numpy(dtype=float))
    atm_vol = float(np.nanmedian(q.loc[q["k"].abs() <= 0.05, "iv_mid"]))
    if not np.isfinite(atm_vol):
        atm_vol = float(np.nanmedian(q["iv_mid"]))
    atm_var = float(np.clip(atm_vol ** 2, 0.005, 0.25))
    lo = np.array([0.0025, 0.15, 0.0025, 0.05, -0.95])
    hi = np.array([0.2500, 8.00, 0.2500, 2.50, 0.30])
    count = {"n": 0}

    def err(p):
        count["n"] += 1
        px, _ = heston_px_mc(is_call, f, k_strike, tau, df, p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3], p[4], mc_steps_per_year, z_s_opt, z_v_opt)
        r = root_wt * (px - y) / eps
        return np.where(np.isfinite(r), r, 1e3)

    starts = [np.array([atm_var, 2.0, atm_var, 0.55, -0.65])]
    best = None
    for p0 in starts:
        t0 = tic()
        res = optimize.least_squares(
            err,
            np.minimum(np.maximum(np.nan_to_num(p0, nan=0.5 * (lo + hi), posinf=hi - 1e-5, neginf=lo + 1e-5), lo + 1e-6), hi - 1e-6),
            bounds=(lo, hi),
            loss="soft_l1",
            f_scale=1.0,
            max_nfev=70,
            xtol=2e-6,
            ftol=2e-6,
        )
        item = {"res": res, "cost": float(res.cost), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
        if best is None or item["cost"] < best["cost"]:
            best = item
    return best["res"].x, best["res"].success, best["seconds"], count["n"], lo, hi

The calibrated Heston parameters are:

\(v_0\approx 0.0117\),
\(\kappa\approx 1.98\),
\(\theta\approx 0.0836\),
\(\xi\approx 1.25\),
\(\rho\approx -0.629\).

The initial volatility implied by \(v_0\) is roughly:
\[
\sqrt{0.0117}\approx 10.8\%
\]
The long-run volatility implied by \(\theta\) is roughly:
\[
\sqrt{0.0836}\approx 28.9\%
\]
So the model says current instantaneous variance is much lower than the long-run variance level needed to explain the option panel. That sounds extreme, but in a short-dated option surface it can happen: the model may use high long-run variance and high vol-of-vol to create skew and convexity even if the current variance starts low.
The Feller ratio is only about 0.212, so the Feller warning is active. This means the fitted process has very high vol-of-vol relative to mean reversion and long-run variance. It is trying hard to fit the smile dynamics with variance randomness.


Heston’s Economic Reading on This SPX Date
The Heston fit implies a market that is calm in current instantaneous variance but still prices substantial future variance risk. That combination often appears when spot markets are calm but option markets still price a nontrivial probability of volatility expansion.
The negative \(\rho\) tells us the model expects bad equity states and high variance states to arrive together. The large \(\xi\) tells us the variance state can move sharply. The low Feller ratio tells us those variance shocks are aggressive enough to push the square-root process near zero in the numerical approximation.
So the Heston fit is saying: the surface wants a strong leverage channel and volatile variance dynamics. It is not saying the surface can be fitted perfectly by Heston. The residual diagnostics already show the fit is weaker than SVI and SABR.


Reading the Heston Parameters Together
The parameters shouldn’t be read one by one in isolation. Their interaction is the model.
The combination of:
\[
v_0\approx 0.0117,\quad \theta\approx 0.0836
\]
means the model starts with low instantaneous variance but expects much higher long-run variance. The combination of:
\[
\xi\approx 1.25,\quad \rho\approx -0.63
\]
means variance shocks are large and strongly negatively correlated with the forward. That creates a steep left skew.
The Feller ratio:
\[
\frac{2\kappa\theta}{\xi^2}\approx 0.21
\]
says the variance process is operating in a high-vol-of-vol regime. In calibration language, the model is stretching the variance process to reproduce option smile convexity. That is a warning about parameter stability, especially if we wanted to use these parameters for long-horizon simulation or risk scenarios.


Discretization Bias and Full Truncation
Euler simulation of square-root variance can produce negative variance if the random shock is large. The continuous-time model is designed for nonnegative variance, but the discrete approximation can step below zero.
The implementation uses a practical protection:
\[
v^+=\max(v,0)
\]
inside square roots and drift terms. Then the simulation update uses \(v^+\) rather than raw \(v\).
This keeps paths numerically valid, but it introduces discretization approximation. With more time steps per year, the approximation improves, but computation becomes slower. This is another reason Monte Carlo Heston is diagnostic here. The model has both parameter uncertainty and numerical uncertainty.
The MC convergence plot helps quantify one side of this. It shows sampling error as paths increase. It doesn’t fully remove discretization bias, but it tells us whether path count is large enough for price noise to be acceptable.
Fit quality is weaker than the best surface models: weighted price RMSE around 3.86, weighted IV RMSE around 0.0149, median absolute IV error around 0.0096, and P90 around 0.0392. The median Monte Carlo standard error is about 0.455 in price units.
This is a key diagnostic point. Heston is theoretically richer than SVI, but it doesn’t automatically fit a single-day quote surface better. SVI is a flexible interpolating smile form. Heston is a low-dimensional stochastic process forced to explain many strikes and maturities through a single variance dynamic. That restriction is valuable for dynamics, but it costs cross-sectional precision.

text:
13) Bates: Heston Plus Jumps
Bates combines Heston stochastic variance with Merton-style jumps. The log-forward update adds a jump term:
\[
d\log F_t=\left(-\frac{1}{2}v_t-\lambda\kappa_J\right)dt+\sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t^F+J_t dN_t
\]
and variance still follows:
\[
dv_t=\kappa(\theta-v_t)dt+\xi\sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t^v
\]
with:
\[
J_t\sim N(\mu_J,\sigma_J^2)
\]
This model has two tail mechanisms:

continuous stochastic variance, where volatility rises and creates fat tails gradually,
jumps, where the underlying can move discontinuously.

The model can use Heston variance to explain persistent skew and term-structure effects, while using jumps to handle short-dated tail prices. That is exactly why Bates is often a useful extension: short-dated OTM options can be too expensive for pure continuous stochastic volatility, while long-dated smile dynamics need more than a one-shot jump distribution.

Nested Model Structure
Bates nests two earlier ideas:
\[
\text{Bates} = \text{Heston stochastic variance} + \text{Merton jumps}
\]
If the jump intensity is zero, Bates collapses toward Heston:
\[
\lambda=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Bates} \approx \text{Heston}
\]
If vol-of-vol is very small and variance is almost constant, the model moves closer to Merton jump-diffusion:
\[
\xi\approx 0,\quad v_t\approx \theta \quad \Rightarrow \quad \text{Bates} \approx \text{Merton-style jump diffusion}
\]
This nesting is useful because the calibration can decide whether the surface needs jumps, stochastic variance, or both. But nesting also creates identification risk. If a left-wing price can be explained by either high jump intensity or very negative spot-vol correlation, the optimizer may find several parameter sets with similar prices.
That is why the implementation starts Bates from Heston and Merton and uses regularization. We want Bates to improve the fit by adding an economically meaningful jump component, not by randomly redistributing error across too many parameters.


Why Bates Improves Fit Without Becoming the Main Signal Model
Bates improves the compact stochastic-panel fit because it has two mechanisms. But better compact-panel fit doesn’t automatically make it better for daily signals.
There are three reasons:

Monte Carlo noise: each Bates price has simulation error.
Parameter identification: jumps and stochastic variance can substitute for each other.
Daily runtime: fitting Bates repeatedly is expensive.

So Bates is best used here as a diagnostic model. If Bates improves tail fit relative to Heston, we learn that jumps are useful. If Bates and Merton agree that jump risk matters, we learn the tail is more discontinuity-driven. But the actual fair-value engine still leans on SVI/SABR because those models are faster, cleaner, and easier to validate daily.
This is a disciplined modeling choice: use the rich model to understand the surface, and use the robust fast models to generate signals.


Bates Calibration and Regularization
Bates has many parameters:
\[
(v_0,\kappa,\theta,\xi,\rho,\lambda,\mu_J,\sigma_J)
\]
More parameters mean more flexibility, but also more calibration risk. The implementation starts from the fitted Heston parameters and fitted Merton jump parameters. It also includes small regularization terms that discourage Bates from moving too far from those starts unless the pricing residuals justify it.
This is important because Heston and jumps can explain similar parts of the smile. For example, left-tail put richness can come from:

very negative \(\rho\) and high \(\xi\) in Heston,
negative jumps with positive intensity in Merton/Bates,
or both.

When two mechanisms explain the same quotes, the calibration becomes weakly identified. Regularization prevents the optimizer from producing extreme parameter combinations that fit the panel but have poor economic stability.


Jump and Volatility Channels in Bates
Bates gives us two different channels for tail pricing.
The continuous stochastic-volatility channel affects many maturities:
\[
v_t \rightarrow I_T=\int_0^T v_sds \rightarrow \text{return dispersion}
\]
The jump channel affects short-dated wings especially strongly:
\[
N_T \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda T)
\]
For small \(T\), the probability of one jump is approximately:
\[
P(N_T=1)\approx \lambda T
\]
So a one-month option with \(\lambda=0.46\) has a one-jump probability around:
\[
0.46\times\frac{1}{12}\approx 3.8\%
\]
That may sound small, but for an OTM put the payoff is concentrated exactly in those rare bad states. A small jump probability can materially raise the option price.
This is the reason Bates often improves short-dated tail fit. Heston can generate fat tails through random variance, but jumps can put probability mass farther into the tail more directly.

def bates_shocks(n_path, n_step, salt):
    n_half = max(int(n_path) // 2, 2)
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed + salt)
    z1 = r.normal(size=(n_half, n_step))
    z2 = r.normal(size=(n_half, n_step))
    zj = r.normal(size=(n_half, n_step))
    uj = r.uniform(size=(n_half, n_step))
    return np.vstack([z1, -z1]).astype(np.float64), np.vstack([z2, -z2]).astype(np.float64), np.vstack([zj, -zj]).astype(np.float64), np.vstack([uj, uj]).astype(np.float64)

@njit(parallel=True)
def bates_px_mc(is_call, fwd, strike, tau, df, v0, kappa, theta, xi, rho, lam, mu_j, sig_j, steps_per_year, z_s, z_v, z_j, u_j):
    n_quote = strike.size
    n_path = z_s.shape[0]
    px = np.empty(n_quote, dtype=np.float64)
    se = np.empty(n_quote, dtype=np.float64)
    rho2 = math.sqrt(max(1.0 - rho * rho, 1e-12))
    kappa_j = math.exp(mu_j + 0.5 * sig_j * sig_j) - 1.0
    for i in prange(n_quote):
        n_step = max(1, int(math.ceil(tau[i] * steps_per_year)))
        dt = tau[i] / n_step
        sqrt_dt = math.sqrt(dt)
        jump_prob = min(max(lam * dt, 0.0), 0.35)
        s1 = 0.0
        s2 = 0.0
        for p in range(n_path):
            log_f = math.log(max(fwd[i], 1e-300))
            v = max(v0, 1e-12)
            for j in range(n_step):
                vp = max(v, 0.0)
                dw_s = z_s[p, j]
                dw_v = rho * z_s[p, j] + rho2 * z_v[p, j]
                jump = 0.0
                if u_j[p, j] < jump_prob:
                    jump = mu_j + sig_j * z_j[p, j]
                log_f += (-0.5 * vp - lam * kappa_j) * dt + math.sqrt(vp) * sqrt_dt * dw_s + jump
                v = v + kappa * (theta - vp) * dt + xi * math.sqrt(vp) * sqrt_dt * dw_v
            ft = math.exp(log_f)
            payoff = max(ft - strike[i], 0.0) if is_call[i] else max(strike[i] - ft, 0.0)
            s1 += payoff
            s2 += payoff * payoff
        mean = s1 / n_path
        var = max(s2 / n_path - mean * mean, 0.0)
        px[i] = df[i] * mean
        se[i] = df[i] * math.sqrt(var / n_path)
    return px, se

        ])
        return np.r_[np.where(np.isfinite(r), r, 1e3), reg]

    starts = [
        np.r_[h0, m0[1], m0[2], m0[3]],
    ]
    best = None
    for p0 in starts:
        t0 = tic()
        res = optimize.least_squares(
            err,
            np.minimum(np.maximum(np.nan_to_num(p0, nan=0.5 * (lo + hi), posinf=hi - 1e-5, neginf=lo + 1e-5), lo + 1e-6), hi - 1e-6),
            bounds=(lo, hi),
            loss="soft_l1",
            f_scale=1.0,
            max_nfev=70,
            xtol=2e-6,
            ftol=2e-6,
        )
        item = {"res": res, "cost": float(res.cost), "seconds": time.perf_counter() - t0}
        if best is None or item["cost"] < best["cost"]:
            best = item
    return best["res"].x, best["res"].success, best["seconds"], count["n"], lo, hi

The fitted Bates parameters are:

\(v_0\approx 0.0108\),
\(\kappa\approx 1.92\),
\(\theta\approx 0.0555\),
\(\xi\approx 1.19\),
\(\rho\approx -0.571\),
\(\lambda\approx 0.459\),
\(\mu_J\approx -0.0396\),
\(\sigma_J\approx 0.0590\).

Compared with Heston, Bates has lower long-run variance and slightly less negative \(\rho\), while the jump component takes part of the tail burden. The jump mean is less negative than in pure Merton, and jump volatility is smaller. This makes sense: once stochastic variance is present, jumps don’t need to explain the entire left wing by themselves.
Fit quality improves materially versus Heston: weighted price RMSE falls to about 2.09, weighted IV RMSE falls to about 0.0090, median absolute IV error is about 0.0053, and P90 IV error is about 0.0217. It is still less accurate than SVI on the full surface, but for the compact stochastic panel Bates is clearly stronger than Heston.


Bates Parameter Reading on This SPX Date
The Bates jump intensity \(\lambda\approx 0.459\) is slightly higher than Merton’s fitted jump intensity, but the average jump size is much less negative. This is an important shift.
Pure Merton had to use larger negative jumps to explain the left tail because it had no stochastic variance. Bates can let stochastic variance handle part of the skew, so jumps become smaller and more frequent/moderate. That is a more balanced decomposition:
\[
\text{left-tail price} = \text{variance channel} + \text{jump channel}
\]
The fitted \(\rho\approx -0.571\) remains strongly negative, so the leverage effect is still active. The jump mean \(\mu_J\approx -0.0396\) corresponds to a typical jump around:
\[
e^{-0.0396}-1\approx -3.9\%
\]
with jump volatility about 5.9%. That is a smaller jump distribution than pure Merton, because Bates no longer needs jumps to explain everything.

That means Bates is better as a diagnostic model here than as the main signal generator.


Bates Residuals Versus Heston Residuals
The Heston-Bates residual comparison is one of the most informative diagnostics in the project. If Bates improves the same quotes where Heston struggles, then jumps are adding useful explanatory power. If Bates improves only through unstable parameters or huge jump intensity, then the improvement may be overfit.
Here Bates improves weighted price and IV errors without hitting parameter bounds. The jump intensity is positive but not extreme, and jump mean/volatility are moderate. That suggests the jump component is being used as a controlled tail adjustment rather than as a wild parameter patch.
Still, Bates remains a compact-panel diagnostic. It isn’t used as the main daily fair-value engine because MC noise and identification risk are too high compared with SVI/SABR.

text:
14) Comparing Models Across Accuracy, Runtime, and Reliability
We now combine all models into a comparison table. This is where the project becomes model-risk-aware.
The fit objective isn’t one-dimensional. A model can be:

accurate but too flexible,
stable but biased,
structural but too slow,
theoretically attractive but weak on the current surface,
useful for diagnostics but risky for trading signals.

The main comparison metrics are:
\[
\text{weighted IV RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i \omega_i(\sigma_i^{model}-\sigma_i^{mkt})^2}{\sum_i\omega_i}}
\]
and:
\[
\text{weighted price RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i \omega_i(V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt})^2}{\sum_i\omega_i}}
\]
We also track:

median absolute IV error,
P90 absolute IV error,
tail error,
calibration time,
objective evaluations,
bound warnings,
suspicious parameter flags,
Monte Carlo warnings.

The goal is to choose which models are safe enough for signals instead of relying only on the lowest table error.

A Model Ranking Needs Several Axes
A useful model ranking needs at least four axes:








Axis
Question
Examples from this project




Accuracy
Does it fit market quotes?
SVI has the best IV RMSE


Structure
Does it encode sensible dynamics?
Heston/Bates have variance processes


Stability
Are parameters away from warnings and bounds?
Heston has a Feller warning


Speed
Can we fit it repeatedly?
SSVI/Merton are fast, MC models are slow



The reason we keep multiple models is that no single axis is enough. SVI is extremely accurate but doesn’t describe a forward variance process. Heston has a true stochastic variance story but fits worse and has Monte Carlo noise. Bates improves stochastic-panel fit but adds identification risk. SABR is fast and structural enough to act as a cross-check.
This multi-axis view is what allows model-risk-aware signal design later. A residual confirmed by SVI and SABR is stronger than a residual generated by a single fragile model.


Cross-Model Disagreement as a Risk Measure
Cross-model disagreement is:
\[
\text{model disagreement}_i=\text{Std}\left(V_{i}^{(1)},V_{i}^{(2)},\ldots,V_{i}^{(M)}\right)
\]
or in IV space:
\[
\text{IV disagreement}_i=\text{Std}\left(\sigma_{i}^{(1)},\sigma_{i}^{(2)},\ldots,\sigma_{i}^{(M)}\right)
\]
If several credible models produce similar fair values, the residual is more trustworthy. If models disagree widely, then the quote may be in a region where assumptions matter more than data.
This is especially important in wings. A deep OTM put can look cheap under SVI but fair under Merton if jump risk is priced differently. Or it can look rich under SSVI because the global model is too rigid. Disagreement tells us to reduce confidence.
In the uncertainty summary, median cross-model IV disagreement is about 0.00262, similar to the median quote IV uncertainty of 0.0025. That means model uncertainty is as important as bid-ask uncertainty for many quotes.

def svi_iv_at(q, p_table):
    vals = []
    for _, row in q.iterrows():
        p = p_table[p_table["expiry"].eq(row["expiry"])]
        if p.empty:
            vals.append(np.nan)
        else:
            pp = p.iloc[0]
            vals.append(float(svi_w(np.array([row["k"]], dtype=float), pp["a"], pp["b"], pp["rho"], pp["m"], pp["sigma"])[0]))
    return np.sqrt(np.maximum(np.asarray(vals, dtype=float), 1e-12) / q["tau"].to_numpy(dtype=float))


def ssvi_iv_at(q, p_frame, theta_table):
    x = q.merge(theta_table[["expiry", "theta_ssvi"]], on="expiry", how="left")
    p = p_frame.iloc[0]
    w = ssvi_w(x["k"].to_numpy(dtype=float), x["theta_ssvi"].to_numpy(dtype=float), p["rho"], p["eta"], p["gamma"])
    return np.sqrt(np.maximum(w, 1e-12) / x["tau"].to_numpy(dtype=float))


def sabr_iv_at(q, p_table, beta):
    vals = np.full(len(q), np.nan, dtype=float)
    for expiry, g in q.groupby("expiry"):
        p = p_table[p_table["expiry"].eq(expiry)]
        if p.empty:
            continue
        pp = p.iloc[0]
        loc = q.index.get_indexer(g.index)
        vals[loc] = sabr_iv_hagan(g["forward"].to_numpy(dtype=float), g["strike"].to_numpy(dtype=float), g["tau"].to_numpy(dtype=float), pp["alpha"], beta, pp["rho"], pp["nu"])
    return vals

The full model comparison is very clear:

SVI dominates raw fit: weighted IV RMSE around 0.00076, median absolute IV error about 0.00034, and P90 about 0.00102.
SABR is second among fast smile models: weighted IV RMSE around 0.00250.
SSVI is much weaker on quote-level fit: weighted IV RMSE around 0.00832.
Bates is the best among the stochastic price-space models on the compact panel, with weighted IV RMSE around 0.00905.
Merton is close to Bates in IV RMSE on the compact panel, around 0.00921, but it lacks stochastic variance.
Heston is weaker here, around 0.01487, with MC and Feller warnings.

On the common benchmark of 54 quotes, the ordering is still similar: SVI is strongest, SABR is strong, Bates improves over Heston, and SSVI remains too rigid for precise quote-level pricing.
This is a strong result, not because one model “wins,” but because each model has a clear role:

SVI is the fair-value core.
SABR is a structural cross-check.
SSVI is a surface discipline check.
Merton, Heston, and Bates are diagnostic engines for jumps and stochastic volatility.

Heston and Bates are expensive because every objective evaluation runs thousands of simulated paths across the compact quote set. The calibration time looks acceptable for one date, but daily historical use would scale quickly. For 500 dates, even 3.5 seconds per calibration becomes roughly half an hour per model before any tuning, plotting, validation, or reruns.
This is why model architecture matters. We use MC stochastic models where they add diagnostic value, and we use fast surface models where repeated daily fair values are needed.

The candidate summary converts model results into operational roles.
A candidate model is accurate and stable enough to contribute to fair values.

A no-signal model is useful for comparison but too noisy, too narrow, or too risky to trade from.
This is a better design than forcing all models into one ensemble. If Heston has a Monte Carlo warning and a Feller warning, giving it a fair-value weight could inject noise into the residual score. If Merton is only a jump bridge, it can help interpret tails without becoming a daily trading model.

section: 15) From Model Fit to Fair Value
text:
15) From Model Fit to Fair Value
We now turn fitted models into fair values. This is the step where a pricing model becomes a possible trading signal.
For each quote, the residual is:
\[
e_i=V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt}
\]
The sign tells us the direction:

\(e_i>0\): the model fair value is above the market mid, so the option looks cheap.
\(e_i<0\): the model fair value is below the market mid, so the option looks rich.

But a raw residual is not enough. We scale it by total uncertainty:
\[
z_i=\frac{e_i}{\epsilon_i}
\]
where \(\epsilon_i\) combines bid-ask spread, model disagreement, and fit/hedge buffers. A larger \(|z_i|\) means the residual is large relative to uncertainty.
The ensemble uses SVI as the main core with capped weights for SABR and SSVI:

SVI weight: 0.70,
SABR weight: about 0.27,
SSVI weight: about 0.03.

This is exactly what the earlier model diagnostics imply. SVI is accurate enough to lead. SABR contributes a structural check. SSVI barely contributes because it is too rigid on the quote-level surface.

Total Error Used for Residual Signals
A raw residual becomes a standardized residual only after we divide by total error:
\[
z_i=\frac{V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt}}{\epsilon_i^{total}}
\]
The total error can include several pieces:
\[
\epsilon_i^{total}=\epsilon_i^{quote}+\epsilon_i^{model}+\epsilon_i^{fit}+\epsilon_i^{hedge}
\]
where:

\(\epsilon_i^{quote}\) comes from bid-ask and vega uncertainty,
\(\epsilon_i^{model}\) comes from disagreement between models,
\(\epsilon_i^{fit}\) comes from calibration fit uncertainty,
\(\epsilon_i^{hedge}\) reflects the fact that the trade will be hedged discretely and with costs.

This is deliberately conservative. A model residual has to beat several sources of uncertainty before it becomes a candidate. That is why the candidate table later filters out most quotes.
For example, suppose an option has model residual \(0.60\), bid-ask half-spread \(0.25\), model disagreement \(0.30\), and hedge buffer \(0.15\). Then total error might be around \(0.70\), so:
\[
z=\frac{0.60}{0.70}\approx 0.86
\]
That is a weak signal. Even though the raw residual looks nontrivial, the uncertainty-adjusted residual is less than one error unit.


Cheap and Rich Signals in Position Direction
The sign of the residual maps into a trade direction.
If:
\[
e_i=V_i^{model}-V_i^{mkt}>0
\]
then the model price is above the market mid. The option looks cheap, so the natural direction is to buy the option:
\[
q_i=+1
\]
If:
\[
e_i<0
\]
then the model price is below the market mid. The option looks rich, so the natural direction is to sell the option:
\[
q_i=-1
\]
But direction is only taken after the residual beats the no-trade filters. A cheap option with a tiny residual isn’t useful. A rich option with high model disagreement isn’t useful. The clean signal is a residual with the right sign, enough magnitude, acceptable spread, and enough historical validation support.
This is why the watchlist is small on the main date. That is a feature of the framework. It is better to reject most apparent mispricings than to trade every curve-fitting residual.


No-Trade Zones Are Part of the Strategy
A no-trade zone is a core part of the design.
The basic no-trade rule is:
\[
|e_i|\le \epsilon_i^{total}
\]
or equivalently:
\[
|z_i|\le 1
\]
When this holds, the residual is inside the combined uncertainty band. Entering a trade there means paying spread and hedge costs for a signal that may be indistinguishable from noise.
The watchlist candidates on the main date have \(|z|\) values below 1, so they are interesting but weak. That is honest. A less disciplined system could force trades by lowering thresholds, but then the backtest would mostly measure noise and costs.
The model-risk-aware approach accepts that many days will have no strong signals. In option relative value, selectivity is a feature.

The anchor/holdout split uses 54 anchor quotes and scores 60 holdout quotes across six expiries. The split is useful because it prevents us from calling a quote cheap just because the model was fitted directly to it. We fit on representative anchors, then score nearby holdout quotes.
The candidate table shows that most apparent residuals are rejected:

41 cheap and 19 rich strict-side observations exist before filters,
36 are inside entry spread,
20 are inside model disagreement,
1 is inside fit or hedge buffer,
only 3 watchlist candidates survive.

That is a strong and honest result. The model stack is not forcing many trades. It is saying that after bid-ask and model uncertainty, very few residuals are large enough to care about on the selected date.
The top watchlist candidates are all modest. The largest displayed cheap call has a price residual around 0.34 with total error around 0.53, so \(z\approx 0.65\). That is a watchlist signal rather than an aggressive trade.


Why Holdout Quotes Matter for Relative Value
If a model is fitted directly to a quote, the residual on that quote is partly in-sample noise. A flexible model can reduce residuals on fitted points even when it has no predictive value. Holdout scoring helps avoid that.
We fit on anchor quotes and score holdout quotes. The holdout residual is closer to a true fair-value estimate because the model had to infer that quote from the surrounding surface. If a holdout quote is far from the model and outside uncertainty bands, it is more interesting than an in-sample residual.
The split also creates a practical trading logic: market makers and relative-value traders often build a smooth surface from liquid anchor points, then look for off-surface quotes away from the anchors. The project implements a simplified version of that idea.

The fair-value plot shows this filtering visually. Raw residuals exist across the surface, but once we account for entry spread and model disagreement, most points sit inside the no-trade zone. This is exactly what model-risk-aware relative value should do. A surface model will always produce residuals because real quotes are noisy. The useful question is whether those residuals exceed the uncertainty required to trade them.


Why the Watchlist Is Small
The small watchlist is a sign that the filters are strict. We start from a fitted surface with thousands of quotes, but after holdout scoring, spread adjustment, model disagreement, and error buffers, only a few quotes survive as watchlist candidates.
This is realistic for liquid SPX options. In a competitive market, obvious model-free mispricings shouldn’t appear everywhere. Most deviations from a fitted model are simply the market’s bid-ask, uncertainty, or a different model assumption.
The small watchlist also protects the later backtest. If the strategy selected hundreds of trades per day, the result would be dominated by correlated exposures and transaction costs. A sparse schedule gives a cleaner test of whether residuals have any useful information.

text:
16) Historical Residual Validation
A model-selected residual only matters if it predicts something out of sample. We therefore fit trade models across historical signal dates and test whether residuals are related to next-day hedged P&L.
The validation object uses a next-day hedged payoff. The idea is:

score a quote at date \(t\),
hold it for one day,
hedge delta exposure,
subtract scheduled costs,
check whether the residual direction predicted the next outcome.

A simple version of the payoff logic is:
\[
\Pi_{t+1}\approx q\,(V_{t+1}-V_t)-q\,\Delta_t(S_{t+1}-S_t)-\text{costs}
\]
where:

\(q\) is position direction and quantity,
\(V\) is option value,
\(\Delta\) is option delta,
\(S\) is underlying spot or hedge instrument.

The delta hedge removes first-order spot exposure, so the remaining P&L is more about volatility, curvature, residual repricing, and model error. It is never perfectly pure because delta changes, volatility moves, spreads matter, and discrete hedging creates tracking error.

Spearman IC and Why Rank Matters
The validation uses rank correlation because residual magnitudes can be noisy. Spearman correlation asks whether larger signals tend to rank with better future outcomes. If \(R(z_i)\) is the rank of the residual score and \(R(\Pi_i)\) is the rank of future hedged payoff, then Spearman correlation is the Pearson correlation of those ranks:
\[
\rho_s=\text{Corr}(R(z_i),R(\Pi_i))
\]
This is more robust than raw correlation when the payoff distribution has outliers. Options have nonlinear payoffs, spreads, and jump moves, so rank-based diagnostics are often more stable.
The daily IC is the same idea applied date by date:
\[
IC_t=\rho_s(z_{i,t},\Pi_{i,t+1})
\]
Then training IC is a rolling estimate of whether the residual direction has recently worked. If training IC is negative, the residual sign is flipped. This is why the strategy can adapt when the model residual behaves more like a contrarian signal than a direct fair-value signal.


Training IC and Direction Learning
The signal direction is learned because residuals can behave in either direction. In theory, if a model says an option is cheap, buying it should make money as price converges upward. In practice, a residual can also indicate a risk premium or model bias. Then the profitable direction may be the opposite.
The rolling training IC estimates this:
\[
\widehat{IC}_{train,t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=t-M}^{t-1}IC_s
\]
The direction can be set as:
\[
d_t=\text{sign}(\widehat{IC}_{train,t})
\]
Then the effective score is:
\[
\tilde{z}_{i,t}=d_t z_{i,t}
\]
If recent IC is negative, the strategy treats raw residuals as contrarian in the opposite direction. This is a very practical idea. It lets the data decide whether model residuals are converging or whether they are systematically pointing the wrong way under the current market microstructure.


Validation Sample Size and Dependence
The validation panel has many rows, but option rows are not independent in the same way stock returns might be. Quotes from the same date and same expiry share the same underlying move, volatility move, and liquidity environment. So 28,415 validation rows don’t mean 28,415 independent experiments.
This is why the daily IC series is important. It aggregates cross-sectional predictive behavior by date. The model can have many quote-level rows but still only about 504 daily environments. If the IC flips sign over time, the strategy has to adapt.
The decile table also has dependence. Options in the same decile can cluster by maturity or option type. So the validation results are evidence, but not final proof. The scheduled trade experiment is a stricter test because it samples a limited number of actual entries with spacing.


Show code
def fit_trade_models(q):
    p_svi, _, _ = fit_svi(q)
    p_sabr, _, _ = fit_sabr(q, primary_beta)
    p_ssvi = pd.DataFrame()
    theta_ssvi = pd.DataFrame()
    if ssvi_ok_for_trade:
        p, theta_ssvi, _, _, _, _, _ = fit_ssvi(q)
        p_ssvi = pd.DataFrame([{"rho": p[0], "eta": p[1], "gamma": p[2]}])
    return p_svi, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi, p_sabr


def score_date(q):
    q_anchor, q_holdout = holdout_split(q)
    if q_anchor.empty or q_holdout.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    p_svi, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi, p_sabr = fit_trade_models(q_anchor)
    out = q_holdout.copy()
    out["svi_iv"] = svi_iv_at(out, p_svi)
    out["svi_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["svi_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
    cols = ["svi_price"]
    if sabr_in_signal:
        out["sabr_iv"] = sabr_iv_at(out, p_sabr, primary_beta)
        out["sabr_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["sabr_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
        cols.append("sabr_price")
    if ssvi_ok_for_trade and not p_ssvi.empty:
        out["ssvi_iv"] = ssvi_iv_at(out, p_ssvi, theta_ssvi)
        out["ssvi_price"] = black76_price(out["option_type"].to_numpy(), out["forward"], out["strike"], out["tau"], out["ssvi_iv"], out["discount_factor"])
        cols.append("ssvi_price")
    weights = np.array([model_wt.get(c.replace("_price", ""), 0.0) for c in cols], dtype=float)
    weights = weights / max(float(weights.sum()), 1e-12)
    out["ensemble_price"] = np.zeros(len(out), dtype=float)
    for c, w in zip(cols, weights):
        out["ensemble_price"] += w * out[c]
    out["model_spread"] = out[cols].std(axis=1).fillna(0.0)
    out["price_residual"] = out["ensemble_price"] - out["mid"]
    out["spread_residual"] = out["price_residual"] / out["half_spread"].replace(0, np.nan)
    out["hedge_buffer"] = 0.0001 * np.abs(out["delta"].fillna(0.0)) * out["forward"] + 0.10 * out["half_spread"]
    out["total_error"] = (out["half_spread"] + 0.5 * out["expected_exit_half_spread"] + 0.5 * out["model_spread"] + out["hedge_buffer"]).clip(lower=0.02)
    out["z_residual"] = out["price_residual"] / out["total_error"].replace(0, np.nan)
    out["strict_candidate"] = out["z_residual"].abs() > 1.0
    out["watchlist_candidate"] = out["z_residual"].abs() > 0.5
    out["candidate"] = out["strict_candidate"]
    out["anchor_quotes"] = len(q_anchor)
    return out

The validation run scores 504 signal dates and creates 28,415 validation rows. The Spearman correlations are negative for all residual scores:

raw residual: about -0.155,
spread-adjusted: about -0.144,
uncertainty-adjusted: about -0.147.

The negative sign means the raw residual direction needs to be interpreted carefully. The training IC column later flips signal direction based on recent performance. The daily IC table shows large variation: some dates have strongly positive IC, others strongly negative. By late 2023 the training IC is around -0.15, so the system learns that the residual should be traded in the opposite direction.
The decile table is more important than one correlation number. Mean next hedged P&L is positive in every decile, but the middle-positive residual deciles have the highest values, with hit rates above 70% in several bins. The highest \(z\) decile has lower mean P&L than mid-high deciles, which warns us that extreme residuals may include more model error or liquidity noise rather than cleaner opportunity.


Interpreting the Non-Monotonic Deciles
The decile table doesn’t show a perfect monotonic edge. That is important. In clean factor research, we often want higher signal deciles to produce higher future returns. Option residual trading is messier.
A mid-level residual can be tradable because it is large enough to matter but still inside a liquid, stable region. An extreme residual can be dangerous because it may come from:

stale quote,
low vega,
jump risk,
wide spread,
model extrapolation,
or a true market premium that doesn’t mean-revert.

So the fact that the middle-high deciles show strong hit rates while the highest decile weakens is economically believable. It tells us to use residuals with cost and model-risk gates rather than just buying the largest absolute residual.

17) Scheduled Delta-Hedged Trading Experiment
After validation, we run a scheduled trading experiment. The goal is to compare two entry selectors:

surface residual selector, which chooses trades based on the model residual logic,
matched ATM baseline, which chooses similar option type, date, sign, and maturity but targets a more ATM-like contract.

The residual strategy schedules up to 80 entries, spaced at least five trading days apart. This prevents the backtest from taking dozens of overlapping signals from the same date and pretending they are independent.
Each trade is held for three days. The backtest evaluates delta-hedged P&L with bid-ask and hedge costs. The delta hedge is meant to reduce directional exposure:
\[
\text{hedge shares}\approx -q\Delta
\]
If we are long one call with \(\Delta=0.45\), we short about \(0.45\) units of the underlying per option multiplier. If the index rises, the call gains but the short hedge loses. The remaining P&L comes from volatility movement, gamma, theta, residual convergence, and execution costs.

Delta-Hedged P&L Through a Taylor Expansion
The delta-hedged P&L can be understood through the option’s local expansion:
\[
dV \approx \Delta dS+\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2+\mathcal{V}d\sigma+\Theta dt+\text{higher-order terms}
\]
If we hedge with \(-\Delta\) units of the underlying, the first-order spot term is reduced:
\[
dV-\Delta dS \approx \frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2+\mathcal{V}d\sigma+\Theta dt+\text{hedging error}
\]
This is why the hedged strategy is still risky. It removes first-order direction, but it leaves:

gamma exposure to realized movement,
vega exposure to implied-volatility changes,
theta decay,
residual convergence or divergence,
re-hedging costs,
bid-ask costs,
discrete hedging error.

A relative-value option signal is usually trying to earn from residual convergence after controlling delta. It is not guaranteed to be positive because gamma/theta/vega can dominate over a short holding period.


Gamma, Theta, and Vega Interactions
A three-day option trade can lose money even when the fair-value residual is correct because the Greeks interact.
If we buy a cheap option, we are usually long gamma and long vega:
\[
\Gamma>0,\quad \mathcal{V}>0
\]
Long gamma benefits from realized movement:
\[
\frac{1}{2}\Gamma(dS)^2
\]
Long vega benefits from implied volatility rising:
\[
\mathcal{V}d\sigma
\]
But long options usually pay theta:
\[
\Theta dt<0
\]
and the bid-ask spread is paid at entry and exit. So the residual has to converge fast enough to beat theta and costs. Short options reverse these exposures: they collect theta but suffer from gamma and vega shocks.
This is why residual trading is difficult. A model can identify a cheap option, but the position still has Greek exposures over the holding window. The hedged backtest is needed because static residual ranking alone can’t answer that.


P&L Components
The attribution is split into:
\[
\Pi_{\text{net}}=\Pi_{\text{option mid}}+\Pi_{\text{delta hedge}}-\text{bid-ask and hedge costs}
\]
where:

\(\Pi_{\text{option mid}}\) is the change in option mid prices,
\(\Pi_{\text{delta hedge}}\) is the P&L from rebalancing the underlying hedge,
costs include option entry/exit spread and hedge trading costs.

This decomposition is important because a strategy can look bad for different reasons:

the option signal can be wrong,
the delta hedge can lose money,
costs can overwhelm a small edge,
the selected options can carry too much vega or gamma risk.

A model-based strategy that produces lower gross loss and lower exposure than the matched baseline can still lose net money if spreads and hedging costs are too large.


Why a Matched Baseline Is Needed
A model-selected option can have a different delta, maturity, spread, and vega than a generic option. If we compare it only against zero, we can’t tell whether the result came from the residual signal or from general option exposure.
The matched baseline solves this by choosing an option with similar broad characteristics but without the residual-selection logic. The comparison asks:
\[
\text{incremental value}=\Pi_{\text{residual selector}}-\Pi_{\text{matched baseline}}
\]
A good residual selector should either:

earn more than the matched baseline,
lose less than the matched baseline,
reduce drawdown for similar exposure,
or show better attribution after hedging.

In the SPX run, it mainly loses less. That is still useful evidence because it means the residual filter is removing some bad exposures, even though it hasn’t created a positive net edge under this simple three-day schedule.

def take_chronological_entries(x, min_gap_days=5, max_entries=80):
    rows = []
    last_date = None
    x = x.sort_values("date").copy()
    for _, r in x.iterrows():

        if last_date is None or (d - last_date).days >= int(min_gap_days):
            rows.append(r)
            last_date = d
        if len(rows) >= int(max_entries):
            break
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).reset_index(drop=True) if rows else pd.DataFrame()

def pick_matched_baseline(day, option_type, target_dte):
    want = day[day["option_type"].eq(option_type)].copy()
    if want.empty:
        return None
    target_dte = float(target_dte) if np.isfinite(target_dte) else 35.0
    lo = max(7.0, target_dte - 10.0)
    hi = min(90.0, target_dte + 10.0)
    d = want[want["dte_days"].between(lo, hi) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.25, 0.75)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        d = want[want["dte_days"].between(max(7.0, target_dte - 18.0), min(90.0, target_dte + 18.0)) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.20, 0.80)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        d = want[want["dte_days"].between(21.0, 60.0) & want["delta"].abs().between(0.20, 0.80)].copy()
    if d.empty:
        return None
    volume = pd.to_numeric(d["volume"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0) if "volume" in d.columns else pd.Series(0.0, index=d.index)
    future = pd.to_numeric(d["future_quote_count"], errors="coerce").fillna(0.0) if "future_quote_count" in d.columns else pd.Series(0.0, index=d.index)
    d["entry_score"] = (
        -2.0 * (d["delta"].abs() - 0.50).abs()
        -0.06 * (d["dte_days"] - target_dte).abs()
        -1.75 * d["relative_spread"].fillna(0.0)
        +0.00015 * volume
        +0.015 * future
    )
    return d.sort_values("entry_score", ascending=False).iloc[0]

def normalized_rows(run_name, result):
    s = summarize_hedging_backtest(result).copy()
    c = result.get("components", pd.DataFrame()).copy()
    if s.empty or c.empty:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    c = c.sort_values(["strategy", "episode_id", "date"])
    first = c.groupby(["strategy", "episode_id"], as_index=False).head(1).copy()
    first["entry_premium"] = (first["main_pos"].abs() * first["option_mid"].abs() * option_multiplier).replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    first["initial_abs_vega"] = first["vega_after"].abs().replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    first["initial_abs_delta"] = first["delta_after"].abs().replace([np.inf, -np.inf], np.nan)
    den = first.groupby("strategy").agg(
        entry_premium=("entry_premium", "sum"),
        initial_abs_vega=("initial_abs_vega", "sum"),
        initial_abs_delta=("initial_abs_delta", "sum"),
        episodes=("episode_id", "nunique"),
    ).reset_index()
    avg_delta = c.groupby("strategy")["delta_after"].apply(lambda x: float(np.nanmean(np.abs(x)))).rename("average_abs_delta").reset_index()
    out = s.merge(den, on="strategy", how="left").merge(avg_delta, on="strategy", how="left")
    out["run"] = run_name
    out["pnl_per_option_premium"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["entry_premium"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_traded_notional"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["traded_notional"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_initial_vega"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["initial_abs_vega"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["pnl_per_average_abs_delta"] = out["total_pnl"] / out["average_abs_delta"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["cost_pct_premium"] = out["total_costs"] / out["entry_premium"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    out["max_drawdown_per_notional"] = out["max_drawdown"] / out["traded_notional"].abs().clip(lower=1e-12)
    return out


normalized_parts = [normalized_rows(run_name, result) for run_name, result in scheduled_results.items()]

The schedule table shows 80 residual entries and 80 matched baseline entries, with a same-type match rate of 100%. That gives a fair comparison: the matched strategy isn’t a random portfolio; it is designed to share broad trade characteristics with the residual schedule.
The hedge-book summary shows 160 scheduled entries and 6,658 hedge-book rows across 159 contracts. The residual strategy and matched strategy both have enough marks to run.
The performance table is sobering:

matched ATM delta strategy loses about $26,621,
surface residual delta strategy loses about $9,032,
both are negative after costs,
the residual strategy has lower drawdown and much lower traded notional.

So the model-selected residual strategy improves materially over the matched ATM baseline, but it still doesn’t produce a positive net strategy in this configuration. That is a much stronger conclusion than simply saying “the model worked.” The signal has some selection value, but trading frictions and short-horizon option noise are still too strong.


Exposure Differences Between Residual and Matched Trades
The matched baseline trades much larger notional than the residual strategy: about $37.37 million traded notional for matched ATM versus about $4.80 million for surface residual. That difference is material. It means the residual selector naturally chooses a different exposure profile.
Mean absolute delta after hedging is also much lower for the residual strategy, around 8.0 versus 28.7. Mean absolute vega is lower too, around 17,677 versus 45,980.
So the residual selector isn’t only changing entry direction. It is changing the risk footprint of selected options. The strategy loses less partly because it takes smaller and more controlled exposures. That is a valid risk-management benefit, even though the net P&L remains negative.


Reading Negative P&L Honestly
The scheduled backtest losing money is not something to hide. It is one of the strongest parts of the project because it prevents overclaiming.
A model can be useful and still fail as a naive trading strategy. The SPX residual selector:

loses much less than the matched baseline,
has lower notional,
has lower absolute delta after hedging,
has lower vega,
has lower total cost,
still loses net money.

That combination says the model is doing some useful selection, but the execution rule is not yet strong enough. Possible reasons include:

three-day horizon is too short or too long,
thresholds are too loose,
spreads are too expensive,
signals are too small,
delta hedging is too crude,
residual direction is unstable.

This kind of diagnosis is much better than tuning parameters until the P&L turns positive. The output gives a realistic research conclusion.
The normalized performance table shows the residual strategy has worse P&L per option premium than the matched baseline, but it uses much less notional and has smaller absolute losses. The cost percentage of premium is higher for the residual strategy, around 3.4% versus 1.8% for the matched baseline, which means it trades options where spreads are more painful relative to premium.
The attribution table is very useful:

matched ATM option mid P&L is about -$17,135,
residual option mid P&L is about -$13,475,
residual delta hedge P&L is much better, around +$8,446 versus +$3,594,
residual costs are much lower, around $3,910 versus $14,372.

This explains why the residual strategy loses less. It isn’t because every option residual converges. It is because the selected trades have better hedge behavior and lower total cost exposure than the matched baseline.
The fixed-hold equity curve plot confirms the table. Both strategies draw down, but the matched ATM baseline loses more and has a much larger drawdown. The residual selector is less damaging and more controlled. That still matters for research: a relative-value model can first prove that it selects better bad trades before it becomes good enough to generate positive trades.
For a production-style version, the next improvements would be tighter entry thresholds, fewer trades, more liquidity constraints, and perhaps longer or adaptive holding windows. We don’t add those here because the point of this project is model comparison and signal validation, not overfitting a trading rule until it looks good.

This matters because Project 11 isn’t just a model demo. It is an end-to-end modeling stack:
